reasons: VERDICT: do not publish. The prose is above average for this dataset -- the foxglove leaf-base tell (blade notched, petiole inserted inside the notch, vs. Digitalis decurrent-winged and no clean boundary) is correct and does not depend on the unreliable woolly-underside test; the Cicuta 'side-veins run to the notches, not the tooth tips' tell is correct; and the 'no preparation of any kind makes a misidentified root safe' framing is exactly right for a root crop. But the entry is encoded against the wrong schema in four places, and two of those defects cause its own deadly warnings to disappear at render time. That alone blocks it.

All 262 lookalike objects across every file in /Users/dmarzari/Server-Sites/Cookbook/data/foraging-research/ use `danger`; this entry uses `severity` on all nine. In /Users/dmarzari/Server-Sites/Cookbook/src/components/ForageSection.tsx: line 69 `const deadly = s.lookalikes.filter((l) => l.danger === 'deadly')` evaluates to an empty array, so the collapsed-row banner 'Confusable with ... -- read before picking.' never renders; that banner is the ONLY warning a user sees without expanding the row. MONTHS ARE OFF BY ONE, AND THE ERROR LANDS ON THE TWO MONTHS THE ENTRY'S OWN PROSE FORBIDS. foraging.ts documents `/** Peak months, 0 = January. */` and `forageFor` filters `s.months.includes(month)`. The convention is unambiguous across all 38 existing entries: chickweed `[0,1,2,3,4,9,10,11]` = Jan-May + Oct-Dec for a winter annual whose prose says 'midwinter is its peak'; Jerusalem artichoke (the other root crop) `[9,10,11,0,1,2]` = Oct-Mar; black walnut `[8,9,10]` = Sep-Nov. This entry's `[2,3,4,9,10,11]` therefore renders as March, April, MAY, October, November, DECEMBER. It drops September, which the entry itself calls the only autumn window in the north 'before the ground frost-locks,' and drops February, the stated opening of the mild-coast window. It adds May, directly against 'stop the moment you see stalks rising' -- second-year burdock is bolting by May across most of the range. It adds December: frozen ground in the north and peak dead-top season, when the above-ground identification this entry makes mandatory cannot be performed. This is a regression: the existing burdock entry in raw.json has `[2,3,8,9,10]` = Mar, Apr, Sep, Oct, Nov, which is correct.

Worse, one array element is a NEGATIVE range statement -- 'Rare to absent: Gulf Coast plain (LA, MS, s. AL, s. GA) and peninsular Florida' -- sitting inside what the data model treats as an INCLUSION list. Any mechanical cleanup that maps it to `southeast` advertises burdock in exactly the region the entry says it is absent from.

THE HARVEST TIMING RULE DEFEATS THE ENTRY'S OWN PRIMARY SAFETY CONTROL. Four lookalikes state that the roots cannot be separated once dug and that the call must be made above ground (Conium: 'a Conium taproot and a burdock taproot are NOT reliably separable'; Cicuta: 'never eat a root you did not personally identify from the intact living plant above ground before you dug it'). But `parts` says to dig 'once the leaves have gone slack' and closes with 'the rule beats the calendar: dig after the tops have died down.' The pokeweed entry then names that exact state -- 'the top has died back to a bare crown and a dead hollow stalk' -- as the most deceptive one. The entry instructs the reader into the condition it elsewhere prohibits.

A DOCUMENTED HAZARD IN THE CURRENT PUBLISHED ENTRY WAS DROPPED WHILE THE NEW TEXT INCREASES EXPOSURE TO IT. The existing raw.json entry warns 'Avoid the mature burs entirely -- the pappus bristles cause severe eye, skin and respiratory irritation.' The revision removes this and instead instructs the forager to 'cut off and bag the burs.' Burdock pappus bristles are a documented cause of conjunctival foreign body and chronic non-healing corneal ulceration (burdock ophthalmia) in humans and animals -- Cole & Su, PeerJ Preprints 1871; conjunctival burdock pappus keratitis case series in the veterinary literature.

THE BELLADONNA CLAIM OVERSTATES ITS OWN CITED SOURCE, and that claim is load-bearing -- it is what the entry offers as proof that belladonna is 'a documented ROOT-level confusion rather than a theoretical one.' Bryson et al. (JAMA 1978) report FDA confirmation of atropine at 30 mg/g (itself a published correction of the original 300 mg/g), but state that how the alkaloid entered the preparation could only be speculation. It was not 'traced to belladonna root harvested and processed with it.' 30 mg/g is 3% by weight, far above the total alkaloid content of belladonna root (~0.3-0.6%), so the figure cited does not support the mechanism asserted.

GOOD, AND WORTH KEEPING ON REWRITE: the statement that burdock root needs no leaching, boiling-off or water changes is correct and the explicit warning that the vinegar soak is cosmetic and 'MUST NOT be read as a detoxifying step' is a genuinely valuable correction; the poison hemlock, comfrey, coltsfoot and pokeweed tells are accurate; the Asteraceae/ragweed cross-reactivity, inulin FODMAP and diuretic/hypoglycaemic cautions match Memorial Sloan Kettering; and the heavy-metal siting guidance (100 ft roadside setback, pre-1978 house sites, lead arsenate orchards, nitrate on manured ground) is sound and is the right call for a taproot.

Scientific name is not wrong, but it is unusable as encoded: `scientific` carries a 400-character essay where every other entry carries a bare binomial.
